mainText:
If you only remember one thing: governments are moving from talking about A I rules to using their legal tools. US states, the F T C, the E U, and Beijing all acted in the same week.

Number one. Regulators close in on Open A I and Anthropic. From your Tech Policy Press newsletter. On Wednesday, eight US states sued Open A I. They say it misled the public about safety, and misused children's data. Tech Policy Press counted thirteen new complaints against the company in one week. The next day, Axios reported that the F T C sent formal demands to Open A I and Anthropic. Each runs over fifty pages. They ask about security incidents, safeguards, and marketing. The E U's A I Office also sent Open A I requests for information on security and outside testing. Open A I says it will cooperate. Why it matters: A I safety claims are now being tested under consumer protection law.

Number two. China's draft A I export controls. From your China A I Weekly Digest. On October sixteenth, Beijing proposed export controls on twenty three A I technologies. These include model weights for very large models, A I agents for sensitive settings, computing clusters, and chip design methods. Access through A P I s and cloud services is exempt, and open source is carved out. Public consultation closes November fifteenth. Why it matters: the tech rivalry now runs in both directions, and weight releases and overseas deployments could be affected.

Number three. A China A I roundup. DeepSeek released a new Flash model with open weights and a one million token context window. DeepSeek is also reportedly leading a seed round in a robotics startup called Winverse A I. Infinigence raised three hundred thirty four million dollars. And StepFun opened the weights of its Step Five preview. Why it matters: open Chinese models keep closing the gap, while money shifts toward robotics.

Number four. A I for good. Fortune ran an essay by Jeannie Annan of the International Rescue Committee. Its Signpost service has reached about twenty million people. Its A I assistant's safety pass rate rose from fifty two to seventy seven percent. It still fails about one answer in four, so a person reviews every response. Why it matters: it's a model for honest, published testing.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker Daily covers the D S A and elections, the Bari Weiss effect on Sixty Minutes, and an interview with John Goodman.

The thread today: safety claims are being audited, and A I is being treated as strategic technology. That's your briefing. Have a good day.
